dek.t: Watching the rise and fall of the abdomen, and noting whatever else takes the mind away from it.

credit.t: These instructions follow the meditation manual of Yuttadhammo Bhikkhu. The technique is the style of insight practice as taught by Ajahn Tong Sirimangalo, in which experience is noted silently and in plain language as it occurs.

runs.t: Sit on the floor with the legs crossed, one leg in front of the other rather than one on top of the other. Rest one hand on top of the other, palms up, in the lap. Keep the back straight, though it does not have to be rigid. Close the eyes.

A chair or a bench works just as well. Sit toward the front of the seat with both feet flat on the floor, and keep the back upright and away from the backrest. If you cannot sit up at all, the same practice can be done lying down.

caption.t: One leg in front of the other, not on top of it. Attention stays on the abdomen.
On a chair, the instructions are unchanged.

runs.t: Place the attention on the abdomen. Breathe normally. Do not deepen, slow or control the breath in any way. You are watching the breathing, not doing it.
As the abdomen rises, note silently in the mind:
. Keep the note in time with the movement, so the word and the sensation happen together, not one before the other.
. This is the home base of the practice. You return to it every time you leave it.

sections.heading: When something else takes your attention

runs.t: The mind will not stay on the abdomen, and it is not supposed to. When something else becomes prominent, leave the abdomen and note what is actually there instead. Repeat the note until the thing fades, then go back to rising and falling. The note is a label, not a judgement: you are naming what is present, not approving of it, arguing with it, or trying to make it stop.
Any thought at all, about the past or the future, pleasant or unpleasant, useful or trivial, gets the same note:
. You do not need to look at the content of the thought.
When a sensation becomes stronger than the breath, note it where it is felt. Pain is the common one: note
and keep noting until it subsides. Do not shift position at the first discomfort, and do not force yourself to sit through real injury.
Pleasant states get noted like everything else:
when the mind settles. Calm is not the goal of the practice and is not a sign that you are doing it correctly. It is simply another thing to be aware of.
The same rule covers whatever else comes up:
. Name it, keep naming it until it passes, then return to the abdomen.

Five to ten minutes is enough at the start. Lengthen it as your capacity grows, rather than by deciding in advance to endure more. Sitting is normally done after walking, and for the same length of time: ten minutes of walking followed by ten minutes of sitting.

paragraphs.t: If you cannot find the rising and falling
place a hand on the abdomen until the movement becomes clear, then take the hand away. If the movement is genuinely not there, note
instead, along with the touch of the body against the floor or the chair.

dek.t: A short straight path, walked slowly, with the note kept in time with the foot.

credit.t: These instructions follow the meditation manual of Yuttadhammo Bhikkhu. The technique is the style of insight practice as taught by Ajahn Tong Sirimangalo, in which experience is noted silently and in plain language as it occurs.

runs.t: Stand with the feet close together, almost touching and level with each other. Neither foot is placed forward, and there is no gap between them. Clasp the hands, the right holding the left, either in front of the body or behind it. Keep the back straight.
The eyes stay open. Let the gaze rest on the path about two metres ahead. Do not watch the feet, and do not look around the room. Looking down bends the neck and pulls the attention out of the body.

caption.t: Eyes open and lowered, hands clasped, back straight.

runs.t: Use a straight path of three to five metres, indoors or outdoors. A path you know well is better than a new one, because there is less to look at. Walk to one end, turn, walk back, the same short path, over and over, for the whole session.

caption.t: The same short path, walked back and forth.

runs.t: Move one foot forward by roughly one foot length, in a single smooth arc from beginning to end. The foot does not stop halfway and does not change direction in the middle. When it lands, the heel of the moving foot is level with the toes of the foot that stayed still.
Note each step in three parts, so the note runs alongside the movement rather than ahead of it or behind it:
as the foot leaves the floor,
as it touches down. So the note is
, on down the path. Go slowly enough that all three parts of the note have somewhere to land. If the note finishes before the foot does, you are walking too fast.

caption.t: Side by side, almost touching, then heel level with the other toes.

runs.t: Do not simply swivel round. The turn is made in stages, a quarter turn at a time. Bring the back foot forward to stand beside the front one, noting
three times, then stand still, noting
three times. Lift the right foot, turn it a quarter turn, place it down, noting
. Bring the left foot beside it the same way, then the right foot again, then the left, which brings you to face back the way you came. Stand still once more, noting

If a thought or feeling comes and goes without pulling you off the path, keep walking and keep noting the steps. If it is strong enough to break the walking, stop where you are: bring the back foot forward, noting
, then note whatever is there the same way as in sitting,
, and so on, until it fades. Then start walking again.

sections.heading: How long, and where it fits

runs.t: Walking comes before sitting, and the two are given the same length of time: ten minutes of walking, then ten minutes of sitting. Walking first is not an arbitrary order. Movement settles the body and gathers the attention while the eyes are still open, so the sitting starts from a mind that is already collected rather than from scratch. In a full session the order is prostration, then walking, then sitting, with the awareness carried unbroken from one to the next.

paragraphs.t: Walking too slowly is as unhelpful as walking too fast. The pace is set by the note, not by an idea of how a meditator should look. Move at whatever speed lets you feel the whole of each step.

dek.t: Three prostrations, made slowly, with every movement noted. The practice that opens a session.

credit.t: These instructions follow the meditation manual of Yuttadhammo Bhikkhu. The technique is the style of insight practice as taught by Ajahn Tong Sirimangalo, in which experience is noted silently and in plain language as it occurs.

runs.t: Kneel down. Either tuck the toes under and sit back on the heels, or rest the tops of the feet on the floor and sit on them, whichever is comfortable enough to keep still in. Rest the hands palm down on the thighs, keep the back straight, and leave the eyes open throughout.

caption.t: Both kneeling positions are correct. Choose the one your knees and ankles allow.

runs.t: Each movement gets one word, said silently three times, once as it begins, once in the middle, once as it ends. A hand rising is noted
, timed to the movement itself. Move slowly enough that this is possible.

caption.t: Palms at the chest, thumbs at the forehead, forehead to the thumbs.

runs.t: From kneeling, hands on the thighs: turn the right hand a quarter turn until it is upright, noting
, then raise it toward the chest, noting
. Do the same with the left hand, so the palms meet with both thumbs at the chest. Raise both hands to the forehead, noting
, then lower them back to the chest.
Bend the back forward to about forty five degrees, noting
. Lower the right hand to the floor in front of the knees, held upright, noting
, until the edge of the little finger touches, noting
, then turn it flat, palm down, noting
. Do the same with the left hand beside it. Bend forward further, bringing the forehead down to the thumbs, noting

caption.t: Thumb tips touching, about 10cm apart. The forehead comes down onto the thumbs, not the floor between them.

sections.heading: Coming up, and the next prostration

runs.t: Raise the back until the arms are straight, noting
. Turn the right hand up onto its edge, noting
, and raise it from the floor to the chest, noting
. Do the same with the left hand, straightening the back upright as you do, so the palms meet at the chest. Raise both hands to the forehead, then lower them to the chest, the same as before.
and prostrate again, so there are three prostrations in all.
After the third prostration, come up through the forehead and chest as above, then lower the hands back to the thighs one at a time, right then left, noting
. Rest a moment, aware of sitting, noting
twice, then come up to standing, noting
twice. Go straight into walking meditation from here, without breaking the awareness in between. The point of finishing carefully is that there is no gap for the mind to slip through.

Thoughts, aches and impatience arise here as they do anywhere else. If something interrupts, pause the sequence, note what is present until it fades, then pick it up where you left it, rather than hurrying to the end of a prostration in order to deal with it afterwards.

paragraphs.t: Three prostrations done this way take several minutes. If you find yourself moving smoothly and quickly through the sequence, the practice has turned into a routine and the noting has stopped doing any work. Slow down until each movement has to be attended to again.
